results.title: Brain region identification
results.question: What are the major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body?
results.response: The major subdivisions of the Drosophila [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") are the calyx, pedunculus, and mushroom body lobe system. This information comes from the Virtual Fly Brain database. VFB records show that the mushroom body is divided into these three parts, with the calyx receiving sensory interneuron afferents, the pedunculus being a thick axon bundle, and the mushroom body lobe system consisting of a vertical branch and a medial branch. VFB holds various data related to the mushroom body, including [602](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in mushroom body") records of neurons with some part in the mushroom body, [176](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,PartsOf "Run in VFB: Parts of mushroom body") records of parts of the mushroom body, and [2](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of mushroom body") records of subclasses of the mushroom body.

results.title: Neuron type classification
results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?
results.response: The adult Drosophila brain contains several types of Kenyon cells. VFB records show that there are subclasses of [Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003686 "Open Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"), including [[KCab-c](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00110929 "Open KCab-c in Virtual Fly Brain")(i)](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049111 "Open KCab-c(i) in Virtual Fly Brain"), KCab-c, [KCg-m](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111061 "Open KCg-m in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Kenyon cell of main calyx](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047926 "Open Kenyon cell of main calyx in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"). Additionally, VFB data indicates that Kenyon cells can be classified into alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells, which can be further subdivided into subtypes such as core/surface/posterior, anterior-posterior/middle, and dorsal/main/gamma-s/gamma-t classes. VFB holds [37](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of Kenyon cell") records of subclasses of Kenyon cell, as well as other data related to Kenyon cells, including images, scRNAseq data, transgene expression, and connectivity classes.

results.title: Neuroanatomy
results.question: What brain regions does the antennal lobe connect to?
results.response:
The [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") connects to the mushroom body and lateral horn. This information comes from the VFB database, which describes antennal lobe projection neurons sending synaptic output to the mushroom body and lateral horn. VFB records show that these neurons generally project to the mushroom body calyx and/or lateral horn. 

VFB holds various data related to the antennal lobe, including a large number of neurons with some part in the antennal lobe, as well as neurons with synaptic terminals, presynaptic terminals, and postsynaptic terminals in the antennal lobe. The database also contains information on parts of the antennal lobe, subclasses of the antennal lobe, and tracts/nerves innervating the antennal lobe. 

To further explore the connections of the antennal lobe, you can examine the available data on neurons with some part in the antennal lobe, or investigate the tracts/nerves innervating the antennal lobe.

results.title: Central complex structure
results.question: What are the main components of the Drosophila central complex and what functions are they associated with?
results.response:
To address the question regarding the main components of the Drosophila central complex and their associated functions, we must consider the structural and functional aspects of this brain region. The Drosophila central complex is a critical area for sensory integration, motor control, and spatial memory. It consists of several distinct substructures, each with specific roles.

The main components include the ellipsoid body, the fan-shaped body, the noduli, and the protocerebral bridge. The ellipsoid body is involved in spatial memory and orientation, while the fan-shaped body is associated with motor control and the regulation of locomotor activity. The noduli and the protocerebral bridge also play significant roles in the integration of sensory information and the coordination of movement.

However, without specific references from the literature or detailed data from databases such as those available in VFB, the precise functions and interactions of these components can only be described in general terms based on my training knowledge. For accurate and detailed information, consulting specific publications or databases focused on Drosophila neuroscience would be necessary.

VFB does not currently hold specific data on the detailed functions of the central complex components. For more detailed insights, it would be beneficial to query the VFB database with specific terms related to the central complex and its substructures or to consult scientific literature that has investigated these aspects of Drosophila neuroscience.

results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response:
The [LPLC2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fva "Open LPLC2 in Virtual Fly Brain") visual neuron type is a type of neuron in the fly brain that detects looming stimuli and elicits a jump escape response. According to VFB, information about LPLC2 is available, and it is described as a Lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron whose cell body lies in the dorsal area of the lateral cell body rind, as noted by Wu et al., 2016. The neuron has a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer, extending outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer, as described by Klapoetke et al., 2017. This arrangement allows it to detect looming, or expansion, stimuli, as reported by Klapoetke et al., 2017. Its activity elicits a jump escape response, as found by Wu et al., 2016, and Klapoetke et al., 2017.

VFB records show that LPLC2 is connected to various neuron types, including sensory system neurons, visual system neurons, and projection neurons. VFB has annotated 610 downstream class-connectivity partners for LPLC2. The specific connections and partners of LPLC2 can be explored further through VFB's connectivity data.

results.title: Shared connectivity
results.question: Do the alpha/beta and gamma Kenyon cells converge on any of the same downstream MBON types? Which MBONs receive input from both?
results.response: The connectome data indicates that alpha/beta Kenyon cells and gamma Kenyon cells converge on the same [mushroom body output neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047953 "Open mushroom body output neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") types. VFB records show that there are shared downstream target classes among these source classes. According to VFB, 13 shared downstream target classes were found among the compared source classes, suggesting that some mushroom body output neurons receive input from both alpha/beta and gamma Kenyon cells. VFB has annotated downstream connectivity classes for alpha/beta Kenyon cells and mushroom body output neurons, which may provide further information on the specific types of mushroom body output neurons that receive input from both.

results.title: Anatomical containment chain
results.question: Trace the anatomical containment hierarchy from the DA1 glomerulus up to the top-level brain structure. What is each level in the hierarchy?
results.response:
The anatomical containment hierarchy from the [antennal lobe glomerulus DA1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003932 "Open antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 in Virtual Fly Brain") up to the top-level brain structure is: antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 -> adult antennal lobe -> adult deutocerebrum -> adult cerebrum -> adult central brain -> adult brain. This information comes from the VFB database, as recorded in the trace containment chain reference. 

VFB holds various records related to the antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, including neurons with some part in it, neurons with synaptic terminals in it, images of neurons with some part in it, and transgene expression in it. However, for the specific hierarchy, the information is derived from the VFB trace containment chain reference. 

To further explore the hierarchy and related data, you can query the VFB database for more information on the adult antennal lobe, adult deutocerebrum, adult cerebrum, adult central brain, and adult brain, as well as the neurons and images associated with the antennal lobe glomerulus DA1.

results.title: Cross-region connectivity
results.question: What neuron types connect the central complex to the lateral accessory lobe, and how strong are these connections?
results.response:
The neuron types that connect the [adult central complex](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003632 "Open adult central complex in Virtual Fly Brain") to the [lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_00050314 "Open lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018 in Virtual Fly Brain") include PFL1, PFL2_PB4, PFL3_PB7, PFL1_PB1, PFL1_PB7, and PFL1_PB2, as recorded in VFB. Additionally, VFB records show that larval mushroom body output neurons, such as c2, f2, and m1, and larval dopaminergic neurons, like DM1b, also connect the central complex to the lateral accessory lobe. 

VFB holds numerous records of neurons with some part in, or synaptic terminals in, both the adult central complex and the lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018, including [363](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003632,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in adult central complex") neurons with some part in adult central complex and [8](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=VFB_00050314,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in embryonic/larval lateral accessory lobe") neurons with some part in embryonic/larval lateral accessory lobe. However, the strength of these connections is not specified in the available data. 

To further investigate the connections between the adult central complex and the lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018, you can explore the available images of neurons with some part in these brain regions, which total [1404](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=VFB_00050314,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in embryonic/larval lateral accessory lobe") for the lateral accessory lobe and [13781](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003632,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in adult central complex") for the adult central complex.

results.title: Experimental planning
results.question: I want to study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila. What neurons are involved, how are they connected, and what genetic tools can I use to access them?
results.response:
To study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila, it is essential to identify the neurons involved and their connections. However, VFB does not currently hold specific data on the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila. 

The connectome data indicates that certain neurons are predicted to be involved in sensory processing and behavior, but the specific neurons and connections involved in CO2 avoidance are not annotated in VFB. 

VFB holds records of various genetic tools that can be used to access neurons in Drosophila, such as GAL4 drivers and split-GAL4 drivers, but it does not currently hold information on which specific tools can be used to access the neurons involved in CO2 avoidance.

To further investigate the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance, you can query the VFB database for neurons and connections involved in sensory processing and behavior, and explore the genetic tools available for accessing these neurons. You may also want to consult the literature for studies on CO2 avoidance in Drosophila, such as those by  Suh et al. (2004) and  Faucher et al. (2006), which may provide more information on the neural circuit underlying this behavior.

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior, as noted by Thomas and Wyman (1984). VFB records show that the giant fiber neuron, also known as DNp01, has a distinct anatomy and connectivity. 

In terms of its anatomy, VFB holds [22](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of DNp01") images of DNp01. The connectome data indicates that DNp01 has downstream connectivity classes ([361](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for DNp01") records) and upstream connectivity classes ([435](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for DNp01") records). 

For genetic manipulation, VFB has annotated [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in DNp01") records of transgene expression in DNp01, which can be used to inform the selection of available driver lines.

Relevant publications, such as the one by Thomas and Wyman (1984), provide further information on the giant fiber neuron's role in jump escape behavior. 

To explore the giant fiber neuron's profile in more detail, you can examine the available images, transgene expression data, and connectivity classes through VFB.

results.title: Hypothesis generation
results.question: Based on connectivity data, what neuron types might mediate a connection between the visual system and the mushroom body? Could visual information reach the memory circuit?
results.response: Based on the connectivity data, neuron types that might mediate a connection between the [visual system](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047735 "Open visual system in Virtual Fly Brain") and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") include [ML-VPN2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052139 "Open ML-VPN2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052141 "Open Mt-VPN1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052140 "Open Mt-VPN in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mti](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052142 "Open Mti in Virtual Fly Brain"), and T4ai. The connectome data indicates that these neurons have some part in the visual system. Additionally, adult visual projection neurons are recorded as having presynaptic terminals in the mushroom body, suggesting they may play a role in mediating this connection. VFB holds records of [1046](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in visual system") neurons with some part in the visual system and [602](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in mushroom body") neurons with some part in the mushroom body, which may be relevant for understanding the potential connection between these two systems. The data suggests that visual information could reach the memory circuit via these neuron types. To further investigate this connection, one could explore the specific tracts and nerves innervating the mushroom body, such as the [adult optic lobe-calycal tract](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00048333 "Open adult optic lobe-calycal tract in Virtual Fly Brain"), which are also annotated in VFB.

results.title: Comparative analysis
results.question: Compare the downstream targets of the two main types of clock neurons (s-LNv and l-LNv). Do they converge on any common target neuron types?
results.response: The downstream targets of [s-LNv](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch03yp "Open s-LNv in Virtual Fly Brain") and [l-LNv](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fws "Open l-LNv in Virtual Fly Brain") include several neuron types. According to VFB, the comparison of downstream targets of s-LNv and l-LNv reveals 17 shared downstream target classes, which include adult interneuron, adult cholinergic neuron, adult GABAergic neuron, adult glutamatergic neuron, adult octopaminergic neuron, adult dopaminergic neuron, and adult serotonergic neuron. This indicates that s-LNv and l-LNv converge on common target neuron types, such as adult cholinergic neuron. VFB holds these data on the downstream targets of s-LNv and l-LNv.

results.title: Novel circuit exploration
results.question: What is the connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the mushroom body? Could temperature information influence memory formation?
results.response:
The connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") is supported by VFB evidence, which suggests that thermosensory projection neurons relay temperature-detecting neurons to higher brain centers, including the mushroom body. This evidence supports a plausible thermosensory influence on mushroom-body memory circuitry through thermosensory projection neurons, as indicated by the VFB query. 

VFB holds various records related to the mushroom body, including neurons with some part in the mushroom body, neurons with synaptic terminals in the mushroom body, and parts of the mushroom body. results.title: Data availability survey
results.question: I'm interested in studying the subesophageal zone (SEZ). How well-characterised is this region in VFB? What neuron types are annotated, what connectomics data is available, and what genetic tools exist for SEZ neurons?
results.response:
The subesophageal zone (SEZ) is characterised in VFB with annotated neuron types, including the [larval subesophageal zone descending SEZ DN neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111241 "Open larval subesophageal zone descending SEZ DN neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"). VFB records show that the SEZ region is well-characterised with specific neuron types annotated, such as the larval subesophageal zone descending SEZ DN neuron, which has its soma located at the level of the subesophageal zone, as described by Ohyama et al., 2015. 

VFB holds 4205 genetic tool/expression pattern rows for the subesophageal zone, indicating that genetic tools exist for SEZ neurons, including GAL4 drivers and binary/intersectional drivers. 

Connectomics data is available for the SEZ, including neurons with parts in the SEZ. VFB has neurons with some part in the SEZ; these can include image-backed connectome or light-microscopy examples. 

To further explore the SEZ, you can query VFB for more information on neuron types, genetic tools, and connectomics data. VFB does not currently hold comprehensive information on all aspects of the SEZ, but the available data can serve as a starting point for investigating this region.

results.title: Graph view regression - medulla region connectivity
results.question: what are the class summarised connectivity from the medulla in graph form
results.response: The [medulla](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003748 "Open medulla in Virtual Fly Brain") is the second optic neuropil, divided into 10 layers. VFB holds data on neurons with some part in medulla, including those with synaptic terminals, presynaptic terminals, and postsynaptic terminals in medulla. Specifically, VFB has annotated [471](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003748,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in medulla") neurons with some part in medulla, [464](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003748,NeuronsSynaptic "Run in VFB: Neurons with synaptic terminals in medulla") neurons with synaptic terminals in medulla, [262](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003748,NeuronsPresynapticHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with presynaptic terminals in medulla") neurons with presynaptic terminals in medulla, and [333](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003748,NeuronsPostsynapticHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with postsynaptic terminals in medulla") neurons with postsynaptic terminals in medulla. The connectome data indicates that these neurons form connections within the medulla, but the exact class summarised connectivity from the medulla is not explicitly stated in the available data. VFB has annotated parts of medulla, tracts/nerves innervating medulla, and lineage clones found in medulla, which may provide further insight into the connectivity of the medulla. To further investigate the class summarised connectivity from the medulla, one could explore the available images of neurons with some part in medulla, transgene expression in medulla, or examine the specific neurons with presynaptic and postsynaptic terminals in medulla.
